section.title: The Sin Offering
section.sectionRationale: The fourth of the five great offerings, the sin offering deals specifically with unintentional sin, scaled to the sinner's position, priest, whole congregation, leader, or common person. It continues the sacrificial law collection, showing that atonement is provided for sin committed even without deliberate intent.
section.thesis: The sin offering provides atonement for unintentional sin according to who has sinned, the anointed priest, the whole congregation, a leader, or an ordinary Israelite, teaching that sin's seriousness and its remedy are measured by the sinner's position and knowledge, yet forgiveness is available to every rank.
section.frameNote: Four movements, one for each category of sinner: the anointed priest, whose sin brings guilt on the whole people; the whole congregation acting in ignorance; the leader; and the common person, each concluding in forgiveness.

units.label: When the anointed priest sins
units.note: guilt spreads to the whole people

verses.text: Then the LORD said to Moses,
“Tell the Israelites to do as follows with one who sins {{shegagah|unintentionally}} against any of the LORD's commandments and does what is forbidden by them:
If the anointed priest sins, bringing guilt on the people, he must bring to the LORD a young bull without blemish as a {{chattat|sin offering}} for the sin he has committed.
He must bring the bull to the entrance to the Tent of Meeting before the LORD, lay his hand on the bull's head, and slaughter it before the LORD.
Then the anointed priest shall take some of the bull's blood and bring it into the Tent of Meeting.
The priest is to dip his finger in the blood and sprinkle some of it seven times before the LORD, in front of the veil of the sanctuary.

The priest must then put some of the blood on the horns of the altar of fragrant incense that is before the LORD in the Tent of Meeting. And he is to pour out the rest of the bull's blood at the base of the altar of burnt offering at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting.
Then he shall remove all the fat from the bull of the sin offering: the fat that covers the entrails, all the fat that is on them,
both kidneys with the fat on them near the loins, and the lobe of the liver, which he is to remove with the kidneys,
just as the fat is removed from the ox of the peace offering. Then the priest shall burn them on the altar of burnt offering.
But the hide of the bull and all its flesh, with its head and legs and its entrails and dung,
all the rest of the bull, he must take outside the camp to a ceremonially clean place where the ashes are poured out, and there he must burn it on a wood fire on the ash heap.

units.label: When the whole congregation strays
units.note: the elders lay hands on the bull

verses.text: Now if the whole congregation of Israel strays unintentionally and the matter escapes the notice of the assembly so that they violate any of the LORD's commandments and incur guilt by doing what is forbidden,
when they become aware of the sin they have committed, then the assembly must bring a young bull as a sin offering and present it before the Tent of Meeting.
The elders of the congregation are to lay their hands on the bull's head before the LORD, and it shall be slaughtered before the LORD.
Then the anointed priest is to bring some of the bull's blood into the Tent of Meeting,
and he is to dip his finger in the blood and sprinkle it seven times before the LORD in front of the veil.

He is also to put some of the blood on the horns of the altar that is before the LORD in the Tent of Meeting, and he must pour out the rest of the blood at the base of the altar of burnt offering at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting.
And he is to remove all the fat from it and burn it on the altar.
He shall offer this bull just as he did the bull for the sin offering; in this way the priest will {{kipper|make atonement}} on their behalf, and they will be forgiven.
Then he is to take the bull outside the camp and burn it, just as he burned the first bull. It is the sin offering for the assembly.
When a leader sins unintentionally and does what is prohibited by any of the commandments of the LORD his God, he incurs guilt.
When he becomes aware of the sin he has committed, he must bring an unblemished male goat as his offering.
He is to lay his hand on the head of the goat and slaughter it at the place where the burnt offering is slaughtered before the LORD. It is a sin offering.
Then the priest is to take some of the blood of the sin offering with his finger, put it on the horns of the altar of burnt offering, and pour out the rest of the blood at the base of the altar.
He must burn all its fat on the altar, like the fat of the peace offerings; thus the priest will make atonement for that man's sin, and he will be forgiven.
And if one of the common people sins unintentionally and does what is prohibited by any of the LORD's commandments, he incurs guilt.
When he becomes aware of the sin he has committed, he must bring an unblemished female goat as his offering for that sin.
He is to lay his hand on the head of the sin offering and slaughter it at the place of the burnt offering.
Then the priest is to take some of its blood with his finger, put it on the horns of the altar of burnt offering, and pour out the rest of the blood at the base of the altar.

Then he is to remove all the fat, just as it is removed from the peace offering, and the priest is to burn it on the altar as a pleasing aroma to the LORD. In this way the priest will make atonement for him, and he will be forgiven.
If, however, he brings a lamb as a sin offering, he must bring an unblemished female.
And he is to lay his hand on the head of the sin offering and slaughter it as a sin offering at the place where the burnt offering is slaughtered.
Then the priest is to take some of the blood of the sin offering with his finger, put it on the horns of the altar of burnt offering, and pour out the rest of its blood at the base of the altar.

And he shall remove all the fat, just as the fat of the lamb is removed from the peace offerings, and he shall burn it on the altar along with the offerings made by fire to the LORD. In this way the priest will make atonement for him for the sin he has committed, and he will be forgiven.

shegagah.gloss: An unintentional sin, an error or straying done without deliberate intent to rebel. This chapter provides atonement precisely for such sins, showing that even unplanned wrongdoing creates real guilt requiring a remedy.

chattat.gloss: The sin offering, from the same root as the word for sin itself. This sacrifice deals directly with the defiling effect of sin on the sanctuary and the sinner's standing before God, unlike the burnt or peace offerings which are more general acts of worship.

kipper.gloss: To atone, to cover. Repeated at the end of every case in this chapter, kaphar describes the priest's mediating action that results, each time, in the sinner being forgiven, nasla, the guilt fully removed.

basic.context: The sin offering, the fourth of the five great sacrifices, deals specifically with sin committed unintentionally, by mistake or ignorance rather than open defiance. The chapter walks through four cases in descending order of impact: the anointed priest, whose sin taints the whole people; the entire congregation; a leader; and finally an ordinary Israelite, each requiring a different animal and each ending in forgiveness.
basic.hermeneutics: This describes Israel's actual old covenant sacrificial system for dealing with unintentional sin; it is not a pattern of animal sacrifice for Christians today. Its abiding truth is that even unintended sin is real sin requiring atonement, and that God has always provided a way for guilty people, whoever they are, to be forgiven.
basic.originalLanguages: The Hebrew shegagah describes an unintentional sin, an error rather than deliberate rebellion, yet it still requires chattat, a sin offering, from the same root as sin itself. Every case in the chapter ends the same way, the priest makes kaphar, atonement, and the sinner is forgiven, nasla, a word meaning the guilt is fully lifted away.
basic.typology: The bull burned entirely outside the camp for the priest's and congregation's sin, its blood taken into the sanctuary itself, foreshadows Christ, who suffered outside the city gate to sanctify His people through His own blood, Hebrews 13:11-12. The sliding scale of offerings by rank pictures a God who deals seriously with every level of sin, from the highest office to the ordinary believer.
basic.christ: Hebrews draws directly on this chapter's pattern: bodies of animals whose blood is brought into the sanctuary are burned outside the camp, and so Jesus also suffered outside the gate to sanctify the people through His own blood, Hebrews 13:11-12. Christ is both the greater priest who mediates atonement and the greater sacrifice whose blood actually cleanses rather than merely covering sin until it is dealt with again.
basic.god: God takes unintentional sin seriously; ignorance of wrongdoing does not remove its guilt or its need for atonement. Yet He also graduates the offering according to what each sinner can bring and their position of responsibility, showing both His justice, which holds leaders to greater account, and His mercy, which forgives every rank fully and completely.
basic.crossReferences: Hebrews 13:11-12 links the sin offering burned outside the camp to Christ's suffering outside the gate. 1 John 1:9 promises that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive us. Psalm 19:12 prays for cleansing from hidden faults, unintentional sins we may not even recognize.
basic.oneStory: The sin offering teaches that unintentional sin still creates real guilt and requires real atonement, whether committed by a priest, the whole nation, a leader, or an ordinary person. This anticipates Christ, whose blood, brought once into the true sanctuary, actually cleanses the conscience of sin, including sins we commit without even realizing it.

context.literary:
Leviticus 4:1 opens with a fresh speech formula, 'Then the LORD said to Moses,' and that formula marks a real turn in the book. Chapters 1 to 3 were framed by a single address, 'When any of you brings an offering,' Leviticus 1:2, and described gifts a worshiper chose to bring. Chapter 4 begins instead with a problem: 'one who sins unintentionally.' The burnt, grain and peace offerings start with the worshiper's desire to draw near; the chattat starts with a breach that has to be repaired.

The chapter is built as four cases laid side by side, and the repetition is the point. Each case follows the same sequence: the sin, the discovery, the animal, the laying on of hands, the slaughter, the handling of the blood, the burning of the fat. Against that fixed frame the reader notices what changes. The first two cases, the anointed priest and the whole congregation, share a bull and the fullest rite: blood carried into the tent, sprinkled seven times before the veil, daubed on the incense altar, and the carcass burned outside the camp. The last two, the leader and the common person, bring smaller animals, and their blood goes no further than the altar of burnt offering in the courtyard.

Small differences carry weight. The case of the anointed priest, verses 3 to 12, is the only one without the closing refrain of atonement and forgiveness that sounds in verses 20, 26, 31 and 35. The leader's case alone opens with 'When' rather than 'If,' verse 22. The phrase 'a pleasing aroma to the LORD' appears in this chapter only once, at the offering of the ordinary Israelite, verse 31. And the common person is given a second option, a lamb instead of a goat, verses 32 to 35, so the chapter ends not at its most solemn point but at its most accessible one.

The chapter then leads straight into Leviticus 5:1-13, which applies the same offering to particular cases and scales it down for the poor, and Leviticus 6:24-30 later gives the priests their side of the same ritual.
context.historical:
The setting is the camp at Sinai, just after the glory of the LORD filled the newly built tabernacle so that even Moses could not enter, Exodus 40:34-35. Leviticus 1:1 has God speaking 'from the Tent of Meeting,' and the question hanging over the book is how a holy God can live in the middle of an unholy camp without consuming it.

The chapter's geography answers part of that question. The tabernacle had three zones: the courtyard with the bronze altar of burnt offering at its entrance, the Holy Place with the golden incense altar, the lampstand and the table, and the Most Holy Place behind the veil. The blood of the sin offering travels as far into that space as the sinner's standing reaches. A leader or commoner defiles the courtyard altar, so the blood goes there. The anointed priest, who ministers inside the tent, and the congregation as a whole, whose sanctuary it is, defile the Holy Place, so the blood is brought inside and sprinkled toward the veil. Only on the Day of Atonement does blood go behind it, Leviticus 16:14-16.

The 'anointed priest' is the high priest, the one 'who has had the anointing oil poured on his head,' Leviticus 21:10. The 'leader' is a tribal chief, the kind of man who led the tribes in presenting gifts at the tabernacle's dedication, Numbers 7:2. 'The common people' renders a phrase that means the people of the land, the ordinary landholding Israelite.

Two details would have struck an Israelite. First, the animals are graded by value: a bull was a major asset, a male goat less, a female goat or lamb less again. Second, 'outside the camp' was normally where the unclean were sent, Leviticus 13:46. Here the remains go to 'a ceremonially clean place,' verse 12, the same ash heap to which the altar's ashes were carried, Leviticus 6:11. The carcass is not rubbish; it is most holy, and it is disposed of with care.
context.canonical:
Numbers 15:22-31 restates this law for the congregation and the individual and then draws the line the chapter assumes but does not state: 'the person who sins defiantly' has no sacrifice, for 'he has despised the word of the LORD,' Numbers 15:30-31. The sin offering is for the straying, not the rebellious.

Within Leviticus the rite reaches its climax on the Day of Atonement, when the same bull and goat are offered and their blood goes behind the veil, their bodies burned outside the camp, Leviticus 16:27. Leviticus 10:16-18 shows the other half of the system: when the blood has not entered the tent, the priests must eat the offering 'to take away the guilt of the congregation.'

The chattat keeps appearing at Israel's turning points. Hezekiah's reform begins with 'a sin offering for the kingdom, for the sanctuary, and for Judah,' 2 Chronicles 29:21, the assembly laying their hands on the goats as the elders do in verse 15. Ezekiel's vision of a restored temple opens with a bull for the sin offering burned outside the sanctuary, Ezekiel 43:19-21, and has the prince provide one 'for himself and for all the people of the land,' Ezekiel 45:22. David prays over the problem this chapter names: 'Who can discern his own errors? Cleanse me from my hidden faults,' Psalm 19:12.

The New Testament uses this chapter with precision. Hebrews says the high priest entered 'for the sins the people had committed in ignorance,' Hebrews 9:7, and that he 'is able to deal gently with those who are ignorant and misguided,' Hebrews 5:2. Hebrews 13:11-12 takes the burning outside the camp and applies it to Jesus outside the city gate. Paul says God sent His Son 'as an offering for sin,' Romans 8:3, the phrase the Greek Old Testament regularly used for this very sacrifice.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses was teaching a newly redeemed people that sin is not only a matter of the heart's intention but a reality that pollutes the place where God lives. The chapter would have unsettled any Israelite who thought that meaning well was enough. A person could break a commandment without knowing it and still 'incur guilt,' verses 13, 22 and 27, and when the matter came to light he was not to shrug but to act.

He also wanted Israel to see that responsibility rises with office. The high priest's sin brings 'guilt on the people,' verse 3, because he stands for them. The leader cannot hide behind his rank; he brings an offering like everyone else. The whole community can err together, and when it does, its elders must own the sin publicly, verse 15.

Above all, Moses wanted the people to know that discovery of sin leads to a door, not a verdict. Every case, once it is known, has a prescribed remedy, and three of the four end with the promise that the sinner 'will be forgiven.' The chapter is written so that a troubled conscience in Israel always had somewhere to go and something to do.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter is prescriptive for Israel: these were binding commands for the priests and people under the Sinai covenant. They are not prescriptive for the church, because Hebrews 10:11-14 teaches that the one offering of Christ has replaced the repeated offerings, and Hebrews 10:18 adds that where sins have been forgiven, 'an offering for sin is no longer needed.'

What carries over is the moral logic. Sins of ignorance are still sins, and a Christian who discovers that he has wronged God or someone else should confess it rather than excuse it as unintended, 1 John 1:9. Leaders are still held to a higher standard, James 3:1. And the church as a body can go wrong together, which is why Christ's letters to the churches in Revelation 2 and 3 call whole congregations to repent. The remedy, though, is no longer an animal but the blood of Christ, applied through confession and faith.

debates.question: Why does the priest's sin, and the sin of the whole congregation, require the same costly bull, while a leader's requires only a goat and a common person's a female goat or lamb?

views.label: Greater office brings greater responsibility
views.case: The anointed priest represents the entire nation before God, so his personal sin corrupts the nation's standing before God, requiring the same weighty remedy as the sin of the whole congregation. Verse 3 says as much: his sin brings 'guilt on the people.'

views.label: The scale reflects proximity to the sanctuary and its holiness
views.case: Others note that the priest's blood is brought further into the sanctuary, before the veil, than the leader's or common person's, whose blood only reaches the altar of burnt offering, suggesting the scale tracks contact with holy space as much as social rank.

debates.bearing: Both readings agree that greater access to and responsibility for God's holy things brings greater accountability, a principle that runs throughout Scripture, compare Luke 12:48 and James 3:1.

debates.question: Does the sin offering cleanse the sinner, the sanctuary, or both?

views.label: It purges the sanctuary
views.case: An influential reading, associated with the Jewish scholar Jacob Milgrom, notes that the blood is never put on the worshiper but always on the altar, the incense altar or toward the veil. On this view sin pollutes God's dwelling like a stain that reaches further in the graver it is, and the chattat cleans the sanctuary so that God can remain. Leviticus 16:16 speaks of atonement 'for the Most Holy Place because of the impurities' of Israel, and the BSB footnote at 4:3 offers 'purification offering.'

views.label: It deals with the sinner's guilt
views.case: Others point out that the chapter repeatedly says the priest makes atonement 'for him' and 'for that man's sin,' verses 26 and 35, and that the result is personal: 'he will be forgiven.' The sinner lays his hand on the animal's head, identifying with it. On this view the sacrifice addresses the person's guilt directly, not only its effects on holy space.

views.label: Both at once
views.case: A third view holds that the two cannot be separated. Sin defiles the sanctuary because it is the sin of people who live around it, so cleansing the sanctuary and forgiving the sinner are one act seen from two sides. The chapter's wording supports both halves.

debates.bearing: The third view best fits the text. Sin in Leviticus is both a personal guilt and a pollution of the place where God meets His people. Hebrews holds the same two together when it says Christ's blood purifies 'our consciences,' Hebrews 9:14, and also the heavenly things themselves, Hebrews 9:23.

study.originalLanguages:
The verb behind the sin offering does more than accuse. In the ordinary stem chata means to miss or to sin, but in the intensive stem the same root means to take sin away, to purify. The BSB shows this when Moses applies the blood to the altar's horns, 'purifying the altar,' Leviticus 8:15, and when David prays, 'Purify me with hyssop,' Psalm 51:7. So the name of the offering holds both the problem and its cure. That double sense explains why a sin offering is also required after childbirth, Leviticus 12:6, and at the end of a Nazirite vow, Numbers 6:14, where no moral fault is in view. Hence the BSB footnote at verse 3: 'Or purification offering.'

The high priest is literally 'the priest, the anointed one,' ha kohen ha mashiach, verses 3, 5 and 16. Mashiach is the word that later becomes Messiah, used of kings such as Saul and David. In Leviticus it names the one man whose sin can bring guilt on the whole people. The chapter thus quietly raises a question the rest of Scripture answers: what if the anointed one were sinless?

The verb asham, 'incur guilt,' recurs in verses 13, 22 and 27, always in the same position, after the sin and before the discovery. Some translators render it 'realize guilt' or 'feel guilty,' because the next clause speaks of the sin becoming known. The BSB's 'incurs guilt' keeps the objective sense, and verses 13 to 14 support it: the guilt exists while the matter 'escapes the notice of the assembly,' and awareness only brings it to light.

The laying on of hands, verses 4, 15, 24, 29 and 33, uses samakh, to lean or press. It is the same gesture Moses uses when he commissions Joshua, Numbers 27:18 and 23, and the gesture Aaron uses over the goat that carries Israel's sins away, Leviticus 16:21. Its core meaning seems to be identification: this animal stands for me.

The chapter's key word for forgiveness, salach, 'he will be forgiven,' has a striking feature: in the Old Testament its subject is always God. People may pardon one another with other words, but this verb is reserved for the LORD. The passive form in verses 20, 26, 31 and 35 is therefore significant. The priest makes atonement, but he never forgives. Forgiveness is God's act alone, which is exactly what the scribes assumed when they asked, 'Who can forgive sins but God alone?' Mark 2:7.

Finally, the two words for the community in verse 13 are worth noticing. 'The whole congregation,' edah, is Israel as the covenant community gathered around the tent; 'the assembly,' qahal, is Israel assembled. The chapter reckons with the possibility that the people of God, not just individuals within it, can go astray together, and it makes the elders answer for the whole, verse 15.

typology.type: The bull's blood brought into the sanctuary, its body burned outside the camp, Leviticus 4:5-12
typology.fulfillment: Hebrews 13:11-12 makes this link itself: the blood goes in, the body goes out, 'and so Jesus also suffered outside the city gate, to sanctify the people by His own blood.' The escalation is twofold. The animal's blood reached only as far as the veil, while Christ entered the Most Holy Place 'once for all by His own blood,' Hebrews 9:12. And the place of disgrace becomes the place of grace, so Hebrews calls believers to 'go to Him outside the camp, bearing the disgrace He bore,' Hebrews 13:13. The type falls short because the burning disposed of a dead animal; Christ's body was raised.

typology.type: The anointed priest who sins and must offer for himself, Leviticus 4:3
typology.fulfillment: Israel's highest mediator could himself be the source of the people's guilt. Hebrews notes that every earthly high priest 'is obligated to offer sacrifices for his own sins, as well as for the sins of the people,' Hebrews 5:3. Christ is the Anointed One who needs no such bull. He is 'holy, innocent, undefiled, set apart from sinners,' and 'does not need to offer daily sacrifices, first for His own sins,' Hebrews 7:26-27. The correspondence lies in the office; the contrast lies in the person. The type shows the need by its failure, pointing to a priest whose sin could never bring guilt on His people.

typology.type: The one who lays his hand on the offering's head, Leviticus 4:29
typology.fulfillment: The worshiper pressed his hand on the animal before killing it, identifying himself with the victim that died in his place. In the gospel the identification runs both ways: God 'made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God,' 2 Corinthians 5:21, and believers are united to Christ in His death, Romans 6:5. The type falls short because the animal was unaware and unwilling. Christ 'offered Himself unblemished to God,' Hebrews 9:14, knowing and choosing the place He took.

typology.type: Atonement graduated by rank, yet available to every level of society, Leviticus 4:3-35
typology.fulfillment: The chapter provides for priest, nation, chief and commoner, and the last case even offers a choice of animal, so no Israelite falls outside the remedy. The gospel keeps the universal reach but removes the gradation. There is one sacrifice for all, 'neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female,' Galatians 3:28, and Christ is 'the atoning sacrifice for our sins, and not only for ours but also for the sins of the whole world,' 1 John 2:2. Here the type falls short by design: rank mattered at the altar, but at the cross the ground is level.

study.christ:
The chapter points to Christ most clearly through the question it leaves open. Its first case concerns 'the anointed priest,' and it is the one case with no closing promise of forgiveness. The man who was supposed to bear the people's sins before God could himself bring guilt on them. Israel's whole system of mediation rested on a flawed mediator. Hebrews builds its argument on exactly this weakness: the law 'appoints as high priests men who are weak; but the oath, which came after the law, appointed the Son, who has been made perfect forever,' Hebrews 7:28. Jesus is the Anointed One whose sin can never bring guilt on His people, because He has none.

The chapter points to Christ through its movement of blood. The graver the sin, the further in the blood must go. That logic reaches its limit in Leviticus 16, when blood goes behind the veil once a year. Hebrews says that arrangement showed 'the way into the Most Holy Place had not yet been disclosed,' Hebrews 9:8. Christ did not carry animal blood a few steps closer; He entered the true sanctuary with His own blood, Hebrews 9:12, and so cleansed not only a tent but 'our consciences from works of death,' Hebrews 9:14.

It points to Christ through the place of burning. Hebrews 13:11-12 notices that the bodies of the most serious sin offerings were burned outside the camp, and that Jesus suffered outside the city gate. The detail is not decoration. The one who carries sin away is carried away from the holy centre, as Jesus was led out of Jerusalem to be crucified.

And it points to Christ through its concern with ignorance. On the cross Jesus prayed, 'Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing,' Luke 23:34. Peter told the crowd in the temple, 'you acted in ignorance, as did your leaders,' Acts 3:17, the very categories of this chapter: people and rulers. Paul said he was shown mercy because he 'had acted in ignorance and unbelief,' 1 Timothy 1:13. The cross is the true sin offering for sins done unknowingly, and it reaches further still, for Christ's blood cleanses 'from all sin,' 1 John 1:7.

The link must be held carefully. Leviticus 4 does not contain a hidden prophecy of Calvary in each detail. The fat, kidneys and liver lobe do not stand for particular virtues of Christ. The connection rests on the New Testament's own reading of the sin offering and on the pattern the chapter itself sets up: a holy God, a polluted dwelling, a substitute, blood, and the word 'forgiven.'
study.god:
This chapter shows God as the one who defines sin. The standard is 'any of the LORD's commandments,' verse 2, not the worshiper's feelings or intentions. A person can do 'what is forbidden' without knowing it, and it is still a real offence, because the measure is God's word and not human awareness. Paul reflects the same conviction: 'My conscience is clear, but that does not vindicate me. It is the Lord who judges me,' 1 Corinthians 4:4.

It shows God's holiness as something that fills space. His presence in the tent is not an idea but a reality that sin affects. The blood's journey toward the veil teaches that sin travels inward to where God dwells, and must be dealt with there. God does not move out when Israel sins; He provides a way to cleanse His house so that He can stay. That is the promise of Leviticus 26:11-12, 'I will make My dwelling place among you,' held in view throughout the book.

It shows God's justice as fair and proportionate. The greater the influence, the greater the offering, so that no one's rank shelters him. The high priest does not get an easier rite than the farmer; he gets a harder one. God is no respecter of persons in judgment, and the chapter proves it by starting at the top.

It shows God's mercy as provided, not merely permitted. He does not wait for Israel to invent a way back. He specifies the animal, the steps and the outcome, and He attaches His own promise: 'they will be forgiven,' verse 20. The forgiveness is His, for the priest only makes atonement. And the rite's final case opens a second option, a lamb instead of a goat, a small sign that God is thinking of what the ordinary worshiper can bring.

These attributes are held together, not traded off. The chapter never softens the reality of sin in order to make room for mercy, and it never withholds mercy in order to make sin look serious. Both are fully present in every case.

For worship, this chapter invites a humble honesty. Believers can pray David's prayer, 'Cleanse me from my hidden faults,' Psalm 19:12, trusting that God cares about what they do not see in themselves, and that He has already provided the cleansing they need in Christ.

crossReferences.note: The companion law to this chapter. It repeats the provision for unintentional sin by the congregation and by individuals, extends it explicitly to the foreigner, and then sets the boundary: the one who sins 'defiantly' blasphemes the LORD and has no sacrifice, 'his guilt remains on him.' It shows why Leviticus 4 speaks only of straying, not rebellion.

The Day of Atonement completes the logic of Leviticus 4. Here the blood of the sin offering goes where no other blood goes, behind the veil to the mercy seat, and atonement is made for the sanctuary itself 'because of the impurities and rebellious acts of the Israelites.' What chapter 4 does case by case, chapter 16 does for the whole year.

Moses is angry when a sin offering is burned rather than eaten, because its blood had not entered the holy place. The passage explains the difference between the cases in Leviticus 4: the offerings of leaders and common people are eaten by the priests 'to take away the guilt of the congregation,' while those whose blood goes inside are burned.

'Who can discern his own errors? Cleanse me from my hidden faults.' The word for errors shares the root of the chapter's term for unintentional sin. David recognises that his own awareness is not a reliable measure of his guilt, and asks God to cleanse what he cannot see, the very situation this chapter was written for.

The high priest entered the Most Holy Place 'for the sins the people had committed in ignorance.' Hebrews reads the whole system of sin offerings, climaxing in the annual rite, as a signal from the Holy Spirit that the way into God's presence had not yet been opened. The sacrifices for ignorance pointed beyond themselves.

The clearest New Testament use of Leviticus 4:12 and 4:21. The bodies of the sin offerings whose blood entered the Holy Place were burned outside the camp, 'and so Jesus also suffered outside the city gate, to sanctify the people by His own blood.' Hebrews then calls believers to go out to Him, bearing His disgrace.

Every high priest 'is able to deal gently with those who are ignorant and misguided,' because he is weak himself and must offer for his own sins. This reads Leviticus 4:3 closely: the anointed priest's need of a sin offering made him sympathetic, but it also exposed the need for a better priest.

Jesus prays, 'Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.' The prayer from the cross takes up the category of sin done in ignorance and brings it to God at the very moment the true sin offering is being made. Forgiveness, God's own act, is asked for those who do not yet see.

Peter tells the crowd, 'you acted in ignorance, as did your leaders,' and then calls them to repent 'so that your sins may be wiped away.' The two groups of Leviticus 4, rulers and people, are named together, and the remedy is no longer a bull or goat but turning to the Christ whom God raised.

God sent His Son 'in the likeness of sinful man, as an offering for sin.' The phrase is the one the Greek Old Testament used for the sin offering throughout Leviticus. Paul presents the incarnation and death of Christ as the chattat that condemns sin in the flesh, doing what the law could not.

John writes so that believers will not sin, but provides for when they do: Jesus Christ the Righteous is both advocate and 'the atoning sacrifice for our sins.' The pairing of a sinless intercessor with a sacrifice answers the flaw of Leviticus 4:3, where the anointed priest himself needed an offering.

study.oneStory:
Genesis 3 left humanity outside the garden, barred from God's presence by cherubim and a flaming sword. Exodus ends with that presence returning to live among a people, the glory filling the tabernacle, Exodus 40:34. The question Leviticus 4 answers is what happens next, when the people God has come to live among keep sinning, often without knowing it. If His presence is to stay, their sin has to be dealt with in the place where He dwells.

This chapter gives the everyday answer. It is not the grand annual ceremony of Leviticus 16 but the ordinary provision for ordinary failure: a leader who discovers he has broken a command, a farmer who realises he has done what was forbidden, a whole community that has drifted. In that sense it shows the patience of God with a people who are redeemed but not yet made new.

Yet the chapter also shows the limits of the arrangement. The anointed priest can himself bring guilt on the nation. The sacrifices must be repeated each time a sin is discovered. The blood reaches only as far as the veil. The prophets later saw that the whole nation had strayed beyond any animal's reach, and Ezekiel's vision of a restored temple still includes a sin offering, Ezekiel 45:22, a sign that the problem was not yet solved.

The story finds its answer in Christ. He is the Anointed One without sin, the offering 'for sin' God Himself sent, Romans 8:3, whose blood goes not toward the veil but into heaven itself, Hebrews 9:24. He suffers outside the gate, and His people follow Him there, Hebrews 13:13. The prayer of the cross, 'Father, forgive them,' covers the ignorant, and the gospel reaches rulers and common people alike.

The story ends in a city with no temple, 'because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple,' Revelation 21:22. There will be no more hidden faults to discover, no more straying to atone for, and no veil left to approach. The dwelling of God with His people, which Leviticus 4 protected one offering at a time, will be permanent, and 'they will see His face,' Revelation 22:4.

quiz.q: What kind of sin does this chapter's sin offering specifically address?

options.text: Sin committed unintentionally, without deliberate intent to rebel.
options.note: Verse 2 explicitly frames the whole chapter around unintentional sin, shegagah.

options.text: Only sins committed in open, deliberate defiance of God.
options.note: The text specifies unintentional sin as its focus, not deliberate rebellion.

options.text: Sins committed only by foreigners living among Israel.
options.note: The chapter addresses priest, congregation, leader, and common Israelite, not foreigners specifically.

options.text: No particular category of sin is in view.
options.note: Verse 2 specifically names unintentional sin as the subject.

quiz.q: What must the anointed priest bring as a sin offering if he sins and brings guilt on the people?

options.text: A young bull without blemish.
options.note: Verse 3 specifies this exact offering for the anointed priest.

options.text: Two turtledoves.
options.note: Birds are the provision for the poor in the guilt offering context, not the required offering here for the priest.

options.text: A female lamb.
options.note: That offering belongs to the ordinary Israelite's case, verse 32, not the anointed priest's.

options.text: No offering is required of the priest.
options.note: Verse 3 explicitly requires a bull from the anointed priest.

quiz.q: Who lays their hands on the bull's head when the whole congregation of Israel sins unintentionally?

options.text: The elders of the congregation.
options.note: Verse 15 specifies the elders performing this act on behalf of the whole assembly.

options.text: Every individual Israelite personally.
options.note: The elders act representatively; not every individual is described as laying hands on the animal.

options.text: The anointed priest alone.
options.note: The priest handles the blood and offering afterward, but the elders lay hands on the bull's head.

options.text: No one lays hands on the offering in this case.
options.note: Verse 15 explicitly describes the elders performing this act.

quiz.q: What offering must a leader, as distinct from a common person, bring for unintentional sin?

options.text: An unblemished male goat.
options.note: Verse 23 specifies a male goat for the leader's sin offering.

options.text: A young bull, the same as the priest.
options.note: The bull is required specifically of the anointed priest and the whole congregation, not the leader.

options.text: A female goat or lamb, the same as a common person.
options.note: Verses 28 and 32 specify female animals for the common person; the leader's offering, verse 23, is a male goat.

options.text: No offering is specified for a leader.
options.note: Verse 23 gives a specific offering for the leader.

quiz.q: What is the consistent outcome stated at the end of each case in this chapter?

options.text: The priest makes atonement for the sinner, and he or they are forgiven.
options.note: This phrase, or a close variant, closes every case, verses 20, 26, 31, and 35.

options.text: The sinner is permanently barred from the camp.
options.note: The chapter describes atonement and forgiveness as the outcome, not permanent exclusion.

options.text: The sinner must repeat the offering seven times.
options.note: The sevenfold sprinkling applies to the blood ritual for the priest and congregation, not a sevenfold repetition of the whole offering.

options.text: No resolution or outcome is given.
options.note: Each case explicitly closes with atonement and forgiveness.

questions: This chapter takes unintentional sin seriously, sin you may not even realize you have committed. Ask God this week to search your heart for blind spots you have not noticed.

The offering required grew or shrank according to the sinner's position and responsibility. Where has God given you influence or responsibility, and are you taking the weight of that seriously before Him?
Every single case in this chapter ends the same way: atonement made, and the sinner forgiven. Do you actually believe you are forgiven, or do you still carry guilt Christ has already dealt with?

The whole congregation could sin together, unnoticed, until someone recognized it. Where might your community, church, or family be collectively blind to a sin that needs to be named and brought to God?

Christ's blood was brought into the true sanctuary once for all, while His body was broken outside the camp. How does knowing His sacrifice actually cleanses your conscience, not merely covers your sin, change how you deal with guilt today?

translationNotes.note: Unintentionally translates shegagah, describing an error or unwitting act; it is contrasted elsewhere in the Torah with sin committed defiantly, or with a high hand, Numbers 15:30, which received no such sacrificial remedy.
Bringing guilt on the people reflects the priest's representative role; his personal failure was understood to affect the whole nation's standing before God, since he ministered on their behalf.

Outside the camp to a ceremonially clean place where the ashes are poured out is the same location where the bodies of these sin offerings were burned, a detail Hebrews 13:11-12 applies directly to Christ's crucifixion outside Jerusalem's gate.
